summary: Describes how the standard ANSI IS-IS and ISO ES-IS routing protocols were implemented inside the NSFNET backbone network. It is an implementation description rather than a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1074 describes how the NSFNET backbone used an adapted form of IS-IS to route traffic internally. It also explains how the backbone exchanged reachability information with attached regional networks through EGP.

subtitle: How the NSFNET backbone adapted IS-IS for internal routing.

tldr.problem: The NSFNET backbone needed an internal routing design that worked across its links and attached regional networks in an IP environment.
tldr.mechanism: The backbone uses a Level 2 subset of IS-IS, computes routes with a shortest-path-first algorithm, and exchanges external reachability through EGP.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents an implementation of ANSI IS-IS and ISO ES-IS in the NSFNET backbone, including adaptations for IP addresses and policy-based routing.

sections.title: Routing in the NSFNET Backbone
sections.content:
The RFC documents an implementation of ANSI IS-IS and ISO ES-IS in the NSFNET backbone. IS-IS serves as the interior gateway protocol inside the backbone, while EGP handles routing exchanges between the backbone and attached mid-level networks.

The memo is an implementation description and continuation of the referenced protocol specifications, not a complete new routing-protocol definition.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS handles routes within the backbone, and EGP carries routing information between the backbone and connected networks. This RFC explains how those protocols were used in that network.

sections.title: Two Levels and Shortest-Path Routing
sections.content:
The underlying IS-IS design has two routing levels: Level 1 handles routes within an area, and Level 2 handles routes between areas. It is a link-state protocol, so each node maintains a topology of the network and computes routes with a modified Dijkstra shortest-path-first algorithm.

The protocol exchanges router and end-system information in Protocol Data Units. The NSFNET backbone implementation described here supports Level 2 routing and permanent point-to-point links.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers share information about network links and use it to build a view of the network. They then calculate a shortest path to destinations.

sections.title: Adapting IS-IS to IP Addresses
sections.content:
IS-IS was designed around OSI network addresses, so the NSFNET implementation places IP addresses inside an NSAP address structure. It sends IS-IS and ES-IS protocol data units over IP, using IP protocol number 85.

EGP reachability learned from regional peers is distributed inside the backbone, with policy-based routing information used to filter and assign costs. The backbone then passes permitted reachability information back to its EGP peers.
sections.plainLanguage: The implementation wraps IP addressing information in the address form IS-IS expects. It also uses routing policy when sharing external routes through the backbone.
